cards.explanation: The answer is that Josiah goes out to confront Neco. Neco, king of Egypt, marches up to fight at Carchemish, and "…Josiah went out to confront him." (2 Chronicles 35:20) A king comes marching up, and Josiah goes out to meet him. Friends, I'd have stayed home and checked on my ovens.

The answer is True. Neco sent messengers to Josiah, saying, "I have not come against you today, but I am fighting another dynasty…" (2 Chronicles 35:21) So the message was that Neco's fight was with another dynasty. Josiah was told this before anything else happened, friends.

The answer is to hurry. Neco says, "…God has told me to hurry." (2 Chronicles 35:21) The man was on a deadline, and then a king stepped in front of him. I know that feeling from a cookie order, friends, but my deadlines never come with an army.

The answer is False. The text says, "Josiah, however, did not turn away from him…" (2 Chronicles 35:22) Neco gave a clear warning, and Josiah kept going anyway. Friends, that "however" is carrying a lot of weight.

The answer is the mouth of God. The text says Josiah "…did not listen to Neco’s words from the mouth of God…" (2 Chronicles 35:22) So the words Neco spoke were from the mouth of God. Josiah did not listen, friends, and he went to fight on the Plain of Megiddo.

The answer is False. Josiah says to his servants, "Take me away, for I am badly wounded!" (2 Chronicles 35:23) There's no "keep fighting" in his words, friends. He was hurt, and he asked to be taken away.

The answer is Jerusalem. His servants "…brought him to Jerusalem, where he died." (2 Chronicles 35:24) They moved him from one chariot to a second chariot and carried him all the way back to the city. Friends, I think that was a long, quiet ride.
The answer is all Judah and Jerusalem. The text says, "…all Judah and Jerusalem mourned for him." (2 Chronicles 35:24) The whole land grieved, friends, and I think it was a heavy day for everyone.

The answer is statute. The singers "…established them as a statute for Israel…" (2 Chronicles 35:25) A statute is a set rule, so these laments weren't a one-time thing, friends. They became a lasting practice in Israel.

The answer is the Book of the Kings of Israel and Judah. The rest of Josiah's acts "…are indeed written in the Book of the Kings of Israel and Judah." (2 Chronicles 35:27) His life, from beginning to end, was written down. Friends, that's a record I'd want to be in.
